title: How to stop Mac notifications from distracting you: Focus and app fixes for macOS 27
metaTitle: How to stop Mac notifications from distracting you (macOS 27)
description: How to stop Mac notifications from distracting you, with Focus, alert styles, schedules and Slack or Teams quiet settings. Costs and causes included.
targetKeyword: how to stop mac notifications from distracting you
intro: To stop Mac notifications from distracting you, set up a Focus in System Settings, let through only the people and apps you need, and quiet the rest. Then tune alert styles and previews app by app. This guide covers what interruptions cost, why macOS keeps pulling you back, and fixes you can use for free.
tldr: Turn on a Focus in System Settings and allow only the people and apps you need.
Set Show previews to Never or When Unlocked, and pick a quiet alert style per app.
Schedule the Focus by time, place or app, so it starts without a manual switch.
Set Slack Do Not Disturb and Teams activity only alerts too, because they have their own rules.
Lazur can point at each setting and guide you one click at a time. It does not click for you.

blocks.text: What interruptions actually cost you

Notifications cost more than the seconds you spend reading them. Each ping asks your attention to move. Then your brain has to return to the task you left. The strongest evidence points to two costs: more mistakes and a worse sense of how your work is going.

Most of that evidence comes from phones, not Macs, and from short lab tasks or one field test. That does not prove your Mac costs you the same. It does show which effects are worth checking on your own desk.

rows: Calls or texts on personal phones during an attention task, in a lab
The increase in mistake probability was more than three times greater than with no notifications. Calls disrupted more than texts.
One assigned day with notifications off across devices, compared with a normal day, 247 analyzed
Fewer interruptions led to higher self-rated performance and lower irritation. The performance effect depended on telepressure.
Aggregated telemetry from Microsoft 365 users, counting meetings, emails and chats
Interruptions about every 2 minutes. This is vendor data, not a survey.
blocks.caption: Three sources on interruptions, and what each one can and cannot show

blocks.text: Ohly and Bastin's field test is the closest thing to a measured fix. People who got fewer notifications reported better performance and less irritation. The test ran for one day, relied on self-reports, and let some people keep a few alerts on. A full workweek with your settings is still untested.

Microsoft's number sounds dramatic, so read it closely. The figure comes from the top 20% of users by ping volume. It counts meetings and chats, not only notifications. Use it as a sign that busy workplaces send many pings, not as a count of your day.
Why the money and grade numbers are missing

You may see large dollar figures and lost-minutes estimates online. We could not open a primary source behind them, so this page leaves them out. We also found no study that tracked course grades in a way we could check. If you want a number for your own week, log your interruptions for a few days before and after a change.
Set up one Focus that fits your workday
A Focus is the main tool here. It decides which apps and people can reach you while it is on. You can create up to ten Focuses, so one can cover deep work and another can cover evenings.

items: Open Apple menu > System Settings > Focus, then pick a Focus or create a new one.
Click Allowed Apps and choose Silence Some Apps. Pick the apps that should stay quiet, such as your chat and mail apps.
Click Allowed People and choose Silence Some People from the Notifications pop-up. Pick the few contacts who may still reach you.
Turn on Time Sensitive Notifications for urgent alerts, then check that the app is allowed to send them in System Settings > Notifications.

blocks.text: Name the Focus after the work, such as Deep work or Review. A clear name makes it easy to pick before you start. Turning a Focus on after the first ping is too late.

blocks.title: Do not allow nothing
blocks.text: A Focus with no allowed people or apps can hide a real emergency. Keep Time Sensitive on for urgent apps and a short list of people who can always reach you.
Schedule the Focus so you stop switching it by hand
A Focus can start on its own. Apple lets it turn on by time of day and days, by location, or when a chosen app opens. Location needs Location Services. The Focus turns off when that app closes.
A schedule removes the daily decision. Match the times to your real calendar, not the hours you wish you kept. A Focus that never runs is only a setting you forgot.

App triggers work well for developers. Start a Focus when Xcode or Cursor opens, so coding time is quiet by default. The Focus turns off when you quit the editor, so it does not carry into the evening.
Tune alerts app by app in Notifications

A Focus controls timing. Notifications settings control how an alert looks. Go to Apple menu > System Settings > Notifications. Under Application Notifications, pick an app to see its alert style and whether it can notify you at all.

Show previews has three options: Always, When Unlocked and Never. Always keeps message text visible even when the Mac is locked. Choose When Unlocked or Never for chat apps if you work in shared spaces.

blocks.title: Banners off, list on
blocks.text: Turn banners off for chat apps and check them on a schedule. You keep the messages and lose the interruption.
Use Slack and Teams quiet settings too

Slack has its own Do Not Disturb. Click the bell icon to snooze alerts for a set time or a custom interval. Type /dnd with a time to do the same from the message box. Slack can also run recurring Do Not Disturb hours if your day has a fixed shape.
Slack's help page does not explain macOS Focus, so set both. Muting a noisy channel is a separate step. Mute the channels you read later, and keep the direct messages you need.

Microsoft Teams works per channel or notification type. You can choose Activity and banner, Activity only, or Off. Activity only keeps alerts in the Activity feed without a banner. In a Focus, add Microsoft Teams under Allowed Apps, then use the Test notification button to check delivery.
Teams' macOS guide describes the option Allow notifications when mirroring or sharing the display. Turn it on if you present often, so banners still appear during a screen share.
A worked example for a developer afternoon

Say you are refactoring a Swift module in Xcode. A teammate posts a review request in Slack, a customer writes in Chrome, and a sprint tool pings about an old ticket. You need to finish the refactor and still catch a real outage.

Your Focus allows Xcode, so build results still come through. It silences Slack channels, Chrome and the sprint tool. Allowed People covers the two contacts who may need you. Where apps support it, their messages can still come through. Time Sensitive Notifications covers outage alerts.
At the end of the block, you open Slack on your schedule. The Focus does the filtering, and you do the choosing.
Mistakes people make with Focus

items: Turning a Focus on and forgetting it. A message from your manager can sit hidden for the rest of the day.
Allowing nobody. A Focus with no allowed people or apps can hide a real emergency.
Leaving previews on in a shared room. Message text then shows on a locked screen.
Treating Slack's Do Not Disturb as the whole fix. Other apps still send alerts to your Mac.
Changing five settings at once. You cannot tell which change helped. Change one setting, then test for a few days.
Copying someone else's Focus. Your allowed list should match your job, not a blog post.

blocks.text: Where Lazur helps, and where it does not

Lazur is a voice assistant for the Mac. Hold ⌥⌘ and ask about anything on screen. Lazur answers out loud and can point at what you ask about. For this problem, it can show you where Focus lives and explain a setting in plain words.
Lazur guides you one click at a time and waits for each click. It does not click buttons, edit files or operate other apps for you. You still flip every switch and choose every rule.

Lazur also helps with the work around the setup. You can set a timer by voice, add an Apple Reminder for your weekly review, or dictate a short note to your team. Hold fn to dictate clean text at the cursor in any app.

Lazur is not a notification filter. It does not sort your alerts, decide which ones matter, or switch your Focus on at the right time. The schedules, previews and app rules stay in System Settings and in each app.
Privacy, and work data you must protect

Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers so Lazur can answer, and they are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models.

blocks.title: Regulated work
blocks.text: If you are a lawyer, nurse, accountant or handle regulated data, follow your employer's rules on client or patient data before you use any voice tool. Check what is on screen before you hold the shortcut.
What to do next

Start with one Focus and one app change, then test for a few days. If Slack is the main source of pings, read the [Slack after hours guide](/for/developers/problems/slack-after-hours-messages-pressure-workers), which covers the habit side. If Slack alerts stop arriving altogether, see [fix missing Slack notifications on Mac](/how-to/fix-missing-notifications-in-slack).

If you live in an editor, the [Cursor guide](/for/developers/cursor) and the [VS Code guide](/for/developers/vs-code) cover shortcuts and setup. When you want to try Lazur, the [download page](/download) has the Mac app, and the [pricing page](/pricing) lists the plans and the trial.

faq.question: Will a Focus block urgent alerts?
faq.answer: It can, unless you allow the app and turn on Time Sensitive Notifications in that Focus. The app also needs permission in System Settings > Notifications. Check both, then send yourself a test message to confirm.

faq.question: Does a Focus also silence Slack and Teams?
faq.answer: A Focus silences the apps you do not allow. Slack and Teams keep their own settings too, so set those as well. Slack has Do Not Disturb and channel mutes. Teams lets you choose Activity only per channel.

faq.question: Is muting a Slack channel the same as a Focus?
faq.answer: No. Muting changes Slack only. A Focus changes what macOS shows across apps while it is on. Use both if Slack is your main source of pings.

faq.question: Will my iPhone follow these settings?
faq.answer: This guide covers the Mac only. Focus settings may sync across your devices, depending on your Apple account setup. Check the iPhone separately before you assume it matches.

faq.question: Can Lazur turn a Focus on for me?
faq.answer: No. Lazur points, explains and guides you one click at a time. It does not click buttons or change settings for you. You turn the Focus on and set its rules.

faq.question: Does Lazur watch my notifications?
faq.answer: Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. It does not sort your notifications or act as a filter for them. You keep control of what reaches you.

faq.question: Does the research show better grades without notifications?
faq.answer: We found no study that tracked course grades in a way we could check. The evidence comes from a lab attention task and a one-day workplace field test. Treat grade claims you see online with care.

faq.question: Do I need Apple Intelligence to use Focus?
faq.answer: No. Focus, Allowed Apps, Allowed People and schedules do not need it. Intelligent Breakthrough and summaries depend on Apple Intelligence, and availability varies by region.

faq.question: What if I still miss messages that matter?
faq.answer: Use Allowed People for the few contacts who must reach you. Keep Time Sensitive on for urgent apps. After a few days, review what got through and adjust one setting at a time.

costs.title: Mistakes on attention tasks
costs.text: In a 2015 lab study, people who got calls or texts on their personal phones made more mistakes on an attention task. The chance of a mistake rose by more than three times compared with people who got no notifications. The study used phones, not Macs. Treat it as a warning sign, not a measure of your own work.

costs.title: Faster work, more strain
costs.text: In a 2008 study of interrupted work, Gloria Mark and colleagues found that people worked faster but reported more stress, frustration and effort. You may finish more tasks and still end the day feeling worse. The summary we opened gives no sample size, so treat it as a direction.

costs.title: Lower self-rated performance
costs.text: In the 2023 Ohly and Bastin field test, fewer notification interruptions led to higher self-rated performance and lower irritation. The performance effect was not the same for everyone. It depended on telepressure, the feeling that you must answer fast.

costs.title: Money and grades are unproven here
costs.text: Online articles quote large dollar figures and lost minutes per switch. We could not open a primary source for them, so this page does not use them. We also found no study that tracked course grades. Measure your own interruptions for a few days before you decide what they cost you.

causes.title: Every ping asks for a glance
causes.text: A notification is a small request to look. The 2015 study found that receiving a notification without responding was about as distracting as answering a call or replying to a text. Ignoring a ping still uses some attention. That is why ignoring alerts does not fully protect your focus.

causes.title: Pings arrive all day
causes.text: Microsoft's WorkLab data says Microsoft 365 users are interrupted about every 2 minutes by meetings, emails or chats. The figure comes from the top 20% of users by ping volume. It is vendor telemetry, not a survey, and it counts more than notifications.

causes.title: Previews show more than you need
causes.text: Mac notifications can show banners, sounds and message text. Show previews can be set to Always, When Unlocked or Never. Always keeps message text visible even on a locked screen, which pulls your eyes and exposes content to people nearby.

causes.title: Each app runs its own rules
causes.text: Slack, Teams and your browser keep their own alert settings. A Mac Focus can silence them, but the apps also control their own alerts. If you change only one place, the other keeps pinging you.

causes.title: Your tolerance for pings varies
causes.text: In the Ohly and Bastin study, interruptions reduced performance at medium and high telepressure, but not at low telepressure. That means the same ping can cost one person much more than another. Notice which alerts make you reply fast, then tune those first.

fixes.title: Set up a Focus with allowed people and apps
fixes.text: Open Apple menu > System Settings > Focus. Create a Focus, then use Allowed Apps and Allowed People to pick what can reach you. This is free and built into macOS. Name the Focus after the work it covers, such as Deep work.

fixes.title: Let urgent alerts through
fixes.text: In the Focus, turn on Time Sensitive Notifications for the apps that must reach you. The app also needs permission in System Settings > Notifications. Without both, urgent alerts can still be hidden from you.

fixes.title: Schedule the Focus by time, place or app
fixes.text: A Focus can turn on by time of day and days, by location (which needs Location Services), or when a chosen app opens. It turns off when that app closes. Schedules remove the daily choice to turn it on.

fixes.title: Set previews and alert styles per app
fixes.text: Go to System Settings > Notifications. Set Show previews to Never or When Unlocked. Under Application Notifications, pick each app's style so chat and mail stay quiet while urgent apps keep banners.

fixes.title: Use Slack's own Do Not Disturb
fixes.text: Click the bell icon in Slack to snooze alerts for a set time, or type /dnd with a time. You can also set recurring Do Not Disturb hours. Muting noisy channels is a separate step, so do that too.

fixes.title: Set Teams to activity only
fixes.text: In Teams, choose Activity only for a channel or notification type, instead of Activity and banner. Add Microsoft Teams under Allowed Apps in each Focus you use. Teams also has a Test notification button to check delivery.

fixes.title: Try breakthrough alerts if your Mac supports them
fixes.text: Apple Intelligence can let important notifications through with Intelligent Breakthrough and Silencing. You turn it on per Focus in System Settings > Focus. It depends on Apple Intelligence, and it is not available in every region.

fixes.title: Turn off apps you never act on
fixes.text: Open System Settings > Notifications and turn off Allow notifications for apps that send alerts you never act on. This is often the quickest fix. You can turn an app back on later, so the change is easy to undo.

plan.label: Day 1
plan.title: List every alert source
plan.text: Open Apple menu > System Settings > Notifications. Scroll the Application Notifications list. Write down the apps that interrupt you and the ones you never act on.

plan.label: Day 2
plan.title: Build one work Focus
plan.text: Create a Focus for deep work. Use Silence Some Apps for chat and mail, and Allowed People for the few contacts who need a fast route to you.

plan.label: Day 3
plan.title: Set previews and alert styles
plan.text: Set Show previews to Never or When Unlocked for chat apps. Turn banners off for apps that only need a glance, and keep them on for urgent alerts you need to see.

plan.label: Day 4
plan.title: Schedule and test urgent alerts
plan.text: Add a schedule or an app trigger to the Focus. Turn on Time Sensitive for urgent apps. If you use Teams, press Test notification to check that banners still arrive.

plan.label: Day 5
plan.title: Review what got through
plan.text: List the alerts that reached you during the week. Keep the settings that helped. Change one thing at a time, so you know what made the difference.
